name: Emeka Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a branch of one of the national tyre and exhaust chains, on the retail park next to the big supermarket. It's drive in, wait in the plastic chairs, drive out: tyres, exhausts, brake pads, batteries, the odd service. On a Saturday I can do twenty sets of tyres before two o'clock. I like that it's simple and you see the job finished in front of you; what wears me out is the targets head office sends down every Monday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What kind of targets, and who are you working with?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Things like how many wiper blades we sell, and how fast the average job is, down to the minute. My manager Phil reads them out like the weather and then ignores half of them. I live with my partner Ruth, who works on the tills at the supermarket next door, and we've got about two months' money put by. I've never used one of those AI things and I don't really see why I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, it was a fad. At work we'd have a laugh about head office's fancy new system that never did anything. I don't post online, so that'd be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means not much changes, which suits me. But head office was already squeezing us with targets before any of this, and they closed the branch in the next town last year. Ruth and I are fine as long as both our wages keep coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep doing my tyres. Maybe put a bit more aside, fifty a month, because two months isn't loads. I wouldn't change anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. There's always a bit of worry with a chain, though, because you never know what the people in head office are thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the branch in the next town closing. What happened to the people there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple got moved to us and the rest took the redundancy. One lad, Simon, ended up stacking shelves at night. A good fitter at the closed branch ended up stacking shelves at night, all because of a spreadsheet at head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could that happen to your branch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could, but we're busier, being next to the supermarket. I'd say it's not likely in the next couple of years. You don't know, though.

say: I'd say AI was **a fad** and laugh about head office's useless new system.
I don't post online, so I'd only say it **at work**.
think: Not much changes, which **suits me**, but head office was squeezing already.
We're fine as long as **both wages** keep coming in.
do: Keep **my head down** and keep fitting tyres as usual.
Put an extra **fifty a month** aside, since two months isn't much.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with a constant low worry about head office decisions.
S0.quote: A good fitter at the closed branch ended up stacking shelves at night, all because of a spreadsheet at head office.
fieldNote: The **closed branch** nearby shapes his sense of risk more than AI.
Relies on **two incomes** with Ruth for security.
Low appetite for change; his plan is to **keep his head down**.

steps.text: Keep fitting tyres at the retail park branch as usual
Put an extra fifty a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, isn't it. Companies will use whatever's cheapest, and you can't really blame them. But I'd also say the government should make sure people get help to move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think head office will love it. Booking, the till, the upsell scripts, the stock ordering, AI does all that, and they'll cut the counter staff first. Then they'll want fitters to do the counter too, faster, with fewer of us. I can see Phil getting a list of names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to learn whatever system they put in, because they wouldn't give me a choice. I'd cut back, no takeaways, no new phone, and save harder. I'd keep an eye on the jobs board but I wouldn't jump unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach. I don't like it when things change and I didn't ask for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fitters would have to do the counter too. How would you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not good. I'm not a talker, I'm a tyre man. If I've got to stand at a screen and answer some AI telling me what to sell, I'd be rubbish at it and they'd know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would go first in your budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways on a Friday, that's forty quid a week. Then I'd keep the old phone instead of upgrading. Ruth would moan about the takeaways more than me.

say: I'd say it's **just business**; firms use whatever's cheapest.
I'd say the **government** should help people move on.
think: Head office will use AI to **cut counter staff** first.
Fewer fitters will cover the counter too, and **Phil** may get a list of names.
do: Learn whatever **till and booking system** head office puts in.
Cut **Friday takeaways** and keep the old phone instead of upgrading.
Watch the **jobs board** without jumping unless forced.
feel: **Uneasy in his stomach**, disliking change he didn't ask for.
S1.quote: I'm not a talker, I'm a tyre man.
fieldNote: He predicts the chain's **counter work** goes first, then fitters stretched thin.
Fears being forced into **selling at a screen**, which he says he'd be bad at.
Calls it **just business**, blaming no one, yet clearly worried.

steps.text: Learn the new booking and till system head office brings in
Stop the forty-pound Friday takeaways and keep the old phone
Check the jobs board weekly without applying yet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's gone too far, too quick, and someone should have slowed it down. I'm not one for protests, but I'd vote for whoever said they'd slow it. At work I'd say, well, that's us done then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think that's my job gone by 2031, maybe sooner. Tyres are already half done by machines, the wheel balancer and the tyre changer, and a robot that can lift a wheel and do the nuts is not science fiction. Before that, by 2028, head office runs the whole place from a computer and they don't need Phil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything we don't need and try to get to four months saved. In the first year after it arrives I'd look for something the robots won't come for soon, maybe driving or warehouse work, though they'd be going too. And I'd talk to my uncle, who's got a little building firm, about labouring for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, really. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums would you be doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent's 800, bills another 300, and if I'm gone it's just Ruth's wage, which is about 1,300. That's nothing left for food. Two months of savings, maybe three, and then what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to your uncle. Would you really go labouring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, yes. It's hard work and it pays less, but robots on a building site are a long way off, I reckon. I'd rather carry blocks than sit at home.

say: I'd say it went **too far, too quick**, and someone should have slowed it.
I'd vote for whoever **promised to slow it**, but wouldn't protest.
think: My tyre job is **gone by 2031**, maybe sooner.
By 2028 head office runs the branch **from a computer** and doesn't need Phil.
do: Cut to essentials and aim for **four months** of savings.
Ask his **uncle's building firm** about labouring work.
Vote for whoever promises to **slow AI down**.
S2.quote: Rent's 800, bills another 300, and if I'm gone it's just Ruth's wage, which is about 1,300.
fieldNote: Gives **exact household sums** and finds no slack without his wage.
Sees tyre fitting as **easy to automate**, already half machine.
Would choose **labouring** over unemployment, despite lower pay.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, bills and food and aim for four months saved
Ask his uncle's building firm about labouring work
Vote for a candidate promising to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, really, that it's going too fast, but at least there's warning this time. I'd say the government should be getting training sorted now. Not that I'd hold my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't change the end for me. Head office goes AI in 2031, and the tyre robots come around 2034. I'd be thirty-four, with no skills except tyres and exhausts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably sit tight for the first couple of years, honestly, because who knows. Then I'd talk to my uncle about the building firm. I'd keep saving whatever we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but a slower worry. Like a leak in the roof you keep meaning to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd sit tight. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, I suppose. I'm not good at moving before I'm pushed. My partner Ruth says I'll wait until the robot's standing in the bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you start earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Phil got told to cut a fitter, I'd move then. Or if Ruth's tills went self-service completely, because then it's both of us. That'd be a kick up the backside.

say: I'd say at least there's **warning** this time.
I'd say the government should **sort training** now, without much hope.
think: Five years **doesn't change the end** for me.
By **2034** I'd be thirty-four with only tyres and exhausts.
do: Sit tight for **the first two years** and see what happens.
Talk to his uncle about **building work** after that.
Keep **saving** whatever the household can spare.
feel: A **slower worry**, like a roof leak he keeps meaning to fix.
S3.quote: My partner Ruth says I'll wait until the robot's standing in the bay.
fieldNote: Admits he **won't move until pushed**; Ruth sees it too.
Both incomes exposed: **self-service tills** threaten Ruth's job.
Expects the **same outcome** as the fast case, only later.

steps.text: Stay on at the tyre branch for the first two years
Talk to his uncle about joining the building firm
Keep saving whatever is left each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning, so nobody can say they weren't told. I'd say people like me should start learning something else. Whether I would, that's another story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be thirty-seven at AGI and forty when the robots come. That's a long way off. I might not even be at the tyre place by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal for a good few years. Maybe, around thirty-two, I'd get my HGV licence to drive lorries, though lorries might be automated too. Mostly I'd wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not too bad. It's far enough away that I can put it to one side most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the HGV licence. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin drives lorries and earns more than me. It's a skill you can take anywhere. But I'd be paying two thousand for a licence for a job that might go too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And would Ruth be part of that decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Course. We'd talk it through at the kitchen table, like with anything big. She's more of a planner than me.

say: I'd say ten years is **fair warning**, so nobody can claim they weren't told.
I'd say people like me should **learn something else**, though I might not.
think: Forty when robots come is **a long way off**.
I might **not even be** at the tyre place by then.
do: Carry on at the tyre branch **as normal** for several years.
Consider an **HGV licence** around thirty-two, despite the two-thousand cost.
feel: **Not too bad**; far enough away to set aside most days.
S4.quote: Ten years is fair warning, so nobody can say they weren't told.
fieldNote: Distance lets him **park the worry**, but he names no firm plan.
HGV idea comes from **his cousin**, yet he doubts it too.
Ruth is the **household planner**; he defers big choices to the kitchen table.

steps.text: Carry on fitting tyres at the retail park branch
Look into a two-thousand-pound HGV lorry licence around age thirty-two

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because it'd catch us with two months' savings and nothing else lined up. What would help is a decent redundancy payment and someone telling me plainly what jobs will still be there. I don't want an app, I want a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the partners. It's not just me, it's Ruth on the tills as well, and we'd both be going at the same time. Everyone talks about one job, but in our house it's two jobs on the same retail park.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about one job, but in our house it's two jobs on the same retail park.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old tyre fitter** at a national chain's retail park branch.
He **never uses AI**, avoids change and prefers to keep his head down.
Pragmatic, he calls automation **just business** and votes rather than protests.
His partner Ruth works the **supermarket tills**, so both household incomes are exposed.
His mood runs from **uneasy to alarmed**, and he rarely acts until pushed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, catching them with two months' savings and no backup plan.
whatWouldHelp: A decent **redundancy payment** and a person, not an app, explaining which jobs remain.
